blocks.text: Topic classification fine-tuning trains a model to identify the subject matter a piece of text discusses, sports, politics, technology, and similar categories, distinct from the intent classification covered in the previous topic, which asks what action a user wants rather than what subject is being discussed.
This topic covers flat versus hierarchical topic taxonomies, the multi-label nature many real topic classification problems have, and the practical challenge of an evolving topic space over time.
1. What Topic Classification Targets

blocks.alt: A news article goes through a topic classifier, producing a topic label like sports, politics, or tech

blocks.text: Topic classification applies the general classification approach, covered in an earlier topic, to categorize text by subject matter, a common application for organizing news articles, documents, or user generated content into meaningful subject categories.
2. Topic vs Intent Classification

blocks.alt: Intent asks what action is wanted while topic asks what subject is discussed

blocks.text: Intent classification, covered in the previous topic, determines what action a user wants performed, topic classification instead determines what subject matter a piece of content concerns, the two tasks share the same underlying classification techniques but answer fundamentally different questions.
3. Flat Lists vs Hierarchical Taxonomies

blocks.alt: A flat topic list is compared against a hierarchical taxonomy

blocks.text: Simple topic classification uses a flat list of categories, sports, politics, technology, side by side with equal standing, more sophisticated systems use a hierarchical taxonomy, technology further split into subtopics like software, hardware, or AI, letting classification happen at whichever level of granularity a use case needs.

blocks.text: 4. Topic Classification as a Multi-Label Problem

blocks.alt: An article about a tech company IPO gets both a technology label and a business label

blocks.text: Many real pieces of content genuinely belong to more than one topic at once, an article about a tech company IPO reasonably belongs to both technology and business, treating topic classification as multi-label, covered generally in the earlier Classification topic, rather than forcing a single topic choice, often better reflects real content.

blocks.text: 5. Handling an Evolving Topic Space

blocks.alt: A new topic emerges against a fixed label set

blocks.text: Topic categories in the real world are not static, new subjects emerge over time, a fixed label set trained once will eventually need updating, either by periodically retraining with an expanded label set or by including a catch-all category for content that does not fit existing topics well.

blocks.title: Static label sets age, sometimes quickly
blocks.content: A topic classifier trained on categories relevant a few years ago may miss entirely new subject areas that have since become significant, periodic review of the label set against current content is worth planning for from the start.

blocks.text: 6. Short Text vs Full Document Topic Classification

blocks.alt: A short headline is compared against a full article body for topic classification

blocks.text: Classifying a short headline provides much less context than classifying a full article body, training data and evaluation should match the actual input length a production system will see, a model trained only on full articles may perform noticeably worse when asked to classify short snippets or headlines alone.
7. Topic Classification Driving Content Systems

blocks.alt: Topic labels drive content routing and a recommendation feed

blocks.text: Predicted topic labels commonly feed directly into downstream systems, routing content to the right section of a publication, or feeding a recommendation feed that surfaces content matching a user known topic interests, making classification accuracy directly consequential for the user experience those systems provide.
8. Evaluating Topic Classifiers

For multi-label topic classification, evaluation needs metrics that account for partial correctness, getting one of two correct topics right is better than getting none right but is not the same as a perfect match, precision, recall, and F1 computed per label, covered generally in the earlier Classification topic, extend naturally to this multi-label case.
9. Common Production Use Cases

Topic classification commonly powers news categorization, content moderation routing, and personalized content recommendation, cases where automatically understanding what a large volume of content is actually about enables organizing or surfacing it effectively at scale.
Worked Example
A news aggregation platform fine-tunes a topic classifier on their existing article archive, initially treating classification as single-label, one topic per article.

Reviewing misclassifications reveals many articles genuinely span multiple topics, business articles with a strong technology angle being routed only to business and missed by users browsing the technology section, switching to multi-label classification and updating their content routing to use all predicted topics rather than just the top one meaningfully improves how well content reaches its intended audience.
Common Mistakes

items: Forcing single-label classification onto content that genuinely spans multiple topics
Training only on full-length documents when production input is often much shorter, like headlines
Letting a fixed topic label set go stale as genuinely new subject areas emerge in the content over time
Evaluating multi-label topic classification with metrics designed for single-label problems

blocks.text: Practice

Pick a piece of content you are familiar with that could reasonably belong to more than one topic category, write out both a forced single-label classification and a multi-label classification for it, and compare which one better reflects the actual content.
Key Takeaway

Topic classification identifies the subject matter of text, distinct from the intent classification covered in the previous topic, and real content often genuinely spans multiple topics, making multi-label framing a better fit than forcing a single choice, while a topic label set itself needs periodic review to keep pace with genuinely new subject areas emerging over time.
